questions.text:
Ravi had ______ younger brother who taught at ______ university. He was widely regarded as ______ honorable man.

Select the option with the correct sequence of articles to fill in the blanks.
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: The article depends on the opening sound, not the letter. "younger" starts with a consonant sound, so "a younger brother". "university" starts with the sound "yoo" (a consonant sound), so "a university". In "honorable" the h is silent and the word starts with a vowel sound, so "an honorable man". The sequence is a; a; an.

questions.text:
The CEO’s decision to downsize the workforce was considered myopic because it sacrificed long-term stability to accommodate short-term gains.

Select the most appropriate option that can replace the word “myopic” without changing the meaning of the sentence.
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: "Myopic" means lacking foresight, seeing only the near term. The sentence confirms it: long-term stability was given up for short-term gains. "Shortsighted" has the same meaning. "Visionary", "progressive" and "innovative" all suggest foresight, the opposite sense.

questions.text: The average marks obtained by a class in an examination were calculated as 30.8. However, while checking the marks entered, the teacher found that the marks of one student were entered incorrectly as 24 instead of 42. After correcting the marks, the average becomes 31.4. How many students does the class have?
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: Correcting the entry raises the total by \(42 - 24 = 18\). The average rises by \(31.4 - 30.8 = 0.6\). So \(n \times 0.6 = 18\), giving \(n = 30\).

questions.text:
Consider the relationships among P, Q, R, S, and T:

- P is the brother of Q.
- S is the daughter of Q.
- T is the sister of S.
- R is the mother of Q.

The following statements are made based on the relationships given above.

(1) R is the grandmother of S.
(2) P is the uncle of S and T.
(3) R has only one son.
(4) Q has only one daughter.

Which one of the following options is correct?
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: R is the mother of Q and S is the daughter of Q, so R is the grandmother of S: (1) is true. T is the sister of S, so T is also a child of Q. P is the brother of Q, so P is the uncle of both S and T: (2) is true. P is a son of R, but the gender of Q is not given, so R may have one or two sons: (3) cannot be concluded. S and T are both daughters of Q, so (4) is false. Hence both (1) and (2) are true.

questions.text:
According to the map shown in the figure, which one of the following statements is correct?

Note: The figure shown is representative.

options.label: A
options.text: The library is located to the northwest of the canteen.

options.label: B
options.text: The hospital is located to the east of the chemistry lab.

options.label: C
options.text: The chemistry lab is to the southeast of physics lab.

options.label: D
options.text: The classrooms and canteen are next to each other.

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: From the map: Library and Physics Lab are north of 5th Cross Road and west of 1st Main Road; Canteen and Hospital are north of the cross road and east of the main road; Hostels and Classrooms are south and west; Chemistry Lab is south and east. (A) The library is level with the canteen, so it is west, not northwest. (B) The hospital is directly north of the chemistry lab, not east. (C) The chemistry lab is south of the cross road and east of the main road, while the physics lab is north and west: southeast is correct. (D) The classrooms are in the south-west block and the canteen in the north-east block, so they are not next to each other.

questions.text:
“I put the brown paper in my pocket along with the chalks, and possibly other things. I suppose every one must have reflected how primeval and how poetical are the things that one carries in one’s pocket: the pocket-knife, for instance the type of all human tools, the infant of the sword. Once I planned to write a book of poems entirely about the things in my pocket. But I found it would be too long: and the age of the great epics is past.”

(From G.K. Chesterton’s “A Piece of Chalk”)

Based only on the information provided in the above passage, which one of the following statements is true?

options.label: A
options.text: The author of the passage carries a mirror in his pocket to reflect upon things.

options.label: B
options.text: The author of the passage had decided to write a poem on epics.

options.label: C
options.text: The pocket-knife is described as the infant of the sword.

options.label: D
options.text: Epics are described as too inconvenient to write.

questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: The passage calls the pocket-knife "the type of all human tools, the infant of the sword", so (C) is stated. (A): "reflected" means thought about; no mirror is mentioned. (B): he planned a book of poems about the things in his pocket, not a poem on epics. (D): he says the book would be too long and the age of great epics is past, not that epics are inconvenient to write.

questions.text:
In the diagram, the lines QR and ST are parallel to each other. The shortest distance between these two lines is half the shortest distance between the point P and line QR. What is the ratio of the area of the triangle PST to the area of the trapezium SQRT?

Note: The figure shown is representative.
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: Let the distance from P to QR be \(h\). The distance between ST and QR is \(\frac{h}{2}\), so the distance from P to ST is also \(\frac{h}{2}\). Since ST is parallel to QR, triangle PST is similar to triangle PQR with ratio \(\frac{1}{2}\), so its area is \(\frac{1}{4}\) of triangle PQR. The trapezium SQRT is the remaining \(\frac{3}{4}\). Ratio \(= \frac{1/4}{3/4} = \frac{1}{3}\).

questions.text: A fair six-faced dice, with the faces labelled ‘1’, ‘2’, ‘3’, ‘4’, ‘5’, and ‘6’, is rolled thrice. What is the probability of rolling ‘6’ exactly once?
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: Choose which of the 3 rolls shows the 6: 3 ways. That roll is 6 with probability \(\frac{1}{6}\) and the other two are not 6 with probability \(\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^2\). So \(P = 3 \times \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{25}{36} = \frac{75}{216}\).

questions.text:
A square paper, shown in figure (I), is folded along the dotted lines as shown in the figures (II) and (III). Then a few cuts are made as shown in figure (IV). Which one of the following patterns will be obtained when the paper is unfolded?

Note: The figures shown are representative.
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: Fold (II) is along the diagonal from top-left to bottom-right, bringing the lower-left half onto the upper-right half. Fold (III) is along the line from the top-right corner to the middle of the long side, giving the small triangle in (IV) whose top edge is the top edge of the square. Unfold step by step. The triangle cut on the top edge (pointing up) reflects across the second fold to the middle of the right edge (pointing right), then across the first fold to the middle of the left edge (pointing left) and of the bottom edge (pointing down). The cut on the left slanted edge lies on the first fold line, so it opens into a full square, and its copy from the second fold gives a second square: one in the upper-left and one in the lower-right. The bar touching the right slanted edge lies on the second fold line, so it opens into a bent (corner) shape near the upper-right corner, and the first fold copies it near the lower-left corner. This is pattern (A). (B) has diamonds instead of squares, (C) has the top and bottom triangles pointing inwards, (D) has a single central square.

questions.text: A shop has 4 distinct flavors of ice-cream. One can purchase any number of scoops of any flavor. The order in which the scoops are purchased is inconsequential. If one wants to purchase 3 scoops of ice-cream, in how many ways can one make that purchase?
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.solution: This is choosing 3 scoops from 4 flavours with repetition allowed and order ignored: \(\binom{n+r-1}{r} = \binom{4+3-1}{3} = \binom{6}{3} = 20\).

questions.text:
Suppose a program is running on a non-pipelined single processor computer system. The computer is connected to an external device that can interrupt the processor asynchronously. The processor needs to execute the interrupt service routine (ISR) to serve this interrupt. The following steps (not necessarily in order) are taken by the processor when the interrupt arrives:

(i) The processor saves the content of the program counter.
(ii) The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR.
(iii) The processor finishes the present instruction.

Which ONE of the following is the CORRECT sequence of steps?
questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.solution: An asynchronous interrupt is recognised only at an instruction boundary, so the processor first finishes the current instruction (iii). It then saves the program counter (i) so the program can resume later. Only after saving can the PC be overwritten with the ISR start address (ii). Order: (iii), (i), (ii).

questions.text: Which ONE of the following statements is FALSE regarding the symbol table?

options.label: A
options.text: Symbol table is responsible for keeping track of the scope of variables.

options.label: B
options.text: Symbol table can be implemented using a binary search tree.

options.label: C
options.text: Symbol table is not required after the parsing phase.

options.label: D
options.text: Symbol table is created during the lexical analysis phase.

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.solution: (A) True: the symbol table records each name with its scope. (B) True: it can be a hash table, a list or a search tree. (D) True: the lexical analyser enters identifiers into it as it meets them. (C) False: semantic analysis (type checking), intermediate code generation and code generation all look up the symbol table after parsing.

questions.text: Which ONE of the following techniques used in compiler code optimization uses live variable analysis?
questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.chapter: Code Optimisation and Data Flow Analysis
questions.solution: Live variable analysis tells at each point which variables will be used later. Register allocation needs exactly this: a register holding a variable that is no longer live can be reused, and two variables that are never live together can share a register. Strength reduction and constant folding work on expressions and induction variables, not liveness, and call management is a runtime matter.

questions.text: Consider a demand paging memory management system with 32-bit logical address, 20-bit physical address, and page size of 2048 bytes. Assuming that the memory is byte addressable, what is the maximum number of entries in the page table?
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution: A page table has one entry per logical page. Page size \(2048 = 2^{11}\) bytes, so the offset takes 11 bits and the page number takes \(32 - 11 = 21\) bits. Number of entries \(= 2^{21}\). The physical address size only affects the width of each entry.

questions.text:
A schedule of three database transactions \(T_1\), \(T_2\), and \(T_3\) is shown. \(R_i(A)\) and \(W_i(A)\) denote read and write of data item \(A\) by transaction \(T_i\), \(i = 1, 2, 3\). The transaction \(T_1\) aborts at the end. Which other transaction(s) will be required to be rolled back?

\[R_1(X) \; W_1(Y) \; R_2(X) \; R_2(Y) \; R_3(Y) \; ABORT(T_1)\]
questions.subject: Databases
questions.solution: \(T_1\) writes \(Y\) and later aborts. \(T_2\) reads \(Y\) after \(W_1(Y)\), and \(T_3\) also reads \(Y\) after \(W_1(Y)\). Both read an uncommitted value written by \(T_1\) (dirty reads). When \(T_1\) aborts, that value never existed, so both \(T_2\) and \(T_3\) must be rolled back (cascading rollback). The read of \(X\) causes no problem because \(T_1\) did not write \(X\).

questions.text:
Identify the ONE CORRECT matching between the OSI layers and their corresponding functionalities as shown.

| OSI Layers | Functionalities |
|---|---|
| (a) Network layer | (I) Packet routing |
| (b) Transport layer | (II) Framing and error handling |
| (c) Datalink layer | (III) Host to host communication |
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.solution: The network layer routes packets: (a)-(I). The transport layer gives end-to-end (host to host) communication: (b)-(III). The data link layer does framing and error handling on a link: (c)-(II).

questions.text:
\(g(.)\) is a function from \(A\) to \(B\), \(f(.)\) is a function from \(B\) to \(C\), and their composition defined as \(f(g(.))\) is a mapping from \(A\) to \(C\).

If \(f(.)\) and \(f(g(.))\) are onto (surjective) functions, which ONE of the following is TRUE about the function \(g(.)\)?

options.label: C
options.text: \(g(.)\) must be a bijective function, that is, both one-to-one and onto.

options.label: D
options.text: \(g(.)\) is not required to be a one-to-one or onto function.

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution: Counterexample: \(A = \{1, 2\}\), \(B = \{p, q, r\}\), \(C = \{x\}\). Let \(g(1) = g(2) = p\) and \(f\) map every element of \(B\) to \(x\). Then \(f\) is onto and \(f(g(.))\) is onto \(C\), yet \(g\) is neither one-to-one (1 and 2 both go to p) nor onto (q, r are missed). So \(g\) need not be injective or surjective.

questions.text: Let \(G\) be any undirected graph with positive edge weights, and \(T\) be a minimum spanning tree of \(G\). For any two vertices, \(u\) and \(v\), let \(d_1(u, v)\) and \(d_2(u, v)\) be the shortest distances between \(u\) and \(v\) in \(G\) and \(T\), respectively. Which ONE of the options is CORRECT for all possible \(G\), \(T\), \(u\) and \(v\)?
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.chapter: Graph Traversals, Spanning Trees and Shortest Paths
questions.solution: \(T\) is a subgraph of \(G\), so the path between \(u\) and \(v\) in \(T\) is also a path in \(G\). Hence the shortest distance in \(G\) can never exceed it: \(d_1 \leq d_2\). Equality need not hold: in a triangle with weights 1, 1, 1.5, the MST drops the 1.5 edge and the distance between its ends becomes 2 in \(T\). (D) fails when \(u\), \(v\) are joined by an MST edge.

questions.text:
Consider the following context-free grammar \(G\), where \(S\), \(A\), and \(B\) are the variables (non-terminals), \(a\) and \(b\) are the terminal symbols, \(S\) is the start variable, and the rules of \(G\) are described as:

\[S \rightarrow aaB \mid Abb\]
\[A \rightarrow a \mid aA\]
\[B \rightarrow b \mid bB\]

Which ONE of the languages \(L(G)\) is accepted by \(G\)?
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.solution: \(A\) generates \(a^n\), \(n \geq 1\), and \(B\) generates \(b^n\), \(n \geq 1\). So \(S \rightarrow aaB\) gives \(a^2 b^n\) and \(S \rightarrow Abb\) gives \(a^n b^2\), each with \(n \geq 1\). \(L(G) = \{a^2 b^n\} \cup \{a^n b^2\}\).

questions.text:
Consider the following recurrence relation:

\[T(n) = 2T(n-1) + n2^n \text{ for } n > 0, \quad T(0) = 1.\]

Which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.solution: Divide by \(2^n\): let \(S(n) = \frac{T(n)}{2^n}\). Then \(S(n) = S(n-1) + n\), \(S(0) = 1\). So \(S(n) = 1 + \frac{n(n+1)}{2}\) and \(T(n) = 2^n\left(1 + \frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right) = \Theta(n^2 2^n)\).

questions.text: Consider the following \(B^+\) tree with 5 nodes, in which a node can store at most 3 key values. The value 23 is now inserted in the \(B^+\) tree. Which of the following options(s) is/are CORRECT?

options.label: A
options.text: None of the nodes will split.

options.label: B
options.text: At least one node will split and redistribute.

options.label: C
options.text: The total number of nodes will remain same.

options.label: D
options.text: The height of the tree will increase.

questions.subject: Databases
questions.solution: 23 is greater than 19, so it goes to the rightmost leaf [20, 21, 22], which is already full (3 keys). The leaf splits into two leaves and a separator key goes up to the root. The root [6, 12, 19] is also full, so it splits too, and a new root is created. (A) False: nodes split. (B) True. (C) False: the node count grows from 5 (two splits plus a new root give 8). (D) True: the new root adds a level.

questions.text: Consider the 3-way handshaking protocol for TCP connection establishment. Let the three packets exchanged during the connection establishment be denoted as P1, P2, and P3, in order. Which of the following option(s) is/are TRUE with respect to TCP header flags that are set in the packets?
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.solution: P1 (client to server) is the SYN segment: SYN = 1, ACK = 0, so (D) is true. P2 (server to client) is SYN+ACK: SYN = 1, ACK = 1, so (B) is true and (C) is false. P3 (client to server) is a pure ACK: SYN = 0, ACK = 1, so (A) is false.

questions.text:
Consider the given system of linear equations for variables \(x\) and \(y\), where \(k\) is a real-valued constant. Which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?

\[x + ky = 1\]
\[kx + y = -1\]

options.label: A
options.text: There is exactly one value of \(k\) for which the above system of equations has no solution.

options.label: B
options.text: There exist an infinite number of values of \(k\) for which the system of equations has no solution.

options.label: C
options.text: There exists exactly one value of \(k\) for which the system of equations has exactly one solution.

options.label: D
options.text: There exists exactly one value of \(k\) for which the system of equations has an infinite number of solutions.

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution: Determinant \(= 1 - k^2\). For \(k \neq \pm 1\) there is exactly one solution, so infinitely many \(k\) give a unique solution and (C) is false. \(k = 1\): \(x + y = 1\) and \(x + y = -1\) contradict, so no solution. \(k = -1\): \(x - y = 1\) and \(-x + y = -1\) are the same line, so infinitely many solutions. Hence exactly one \(k\) gives no solution (A true, B false) and exactly one \(k\) gives infinitely many (D true).

questions.text: Let \(X\) be a 3-variable Boolean function that produces output as ‘1’ when at least two of the input variables are ‘1’. Which of the following statement(s) is/are CORRECT, where \(a, b, c, d, e\) are Boolean variables?

options.label: A
options.text: \(X(a, b, X(c, d, e)) = X(X(a, b, c), d, e)\)

options.label: C
options.text: \(X(a, b, X(a, c, d)) = (X(a, b, a) \text{ AND } X(c, d, c))\)

options.label: D
options.text: \(X(a, b, c) = X(a, X(a, b, c), X(a, c, c))\)

questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.solution: \(X\) is the majority function, and \(X(p, p, q) = p\). (A) False: take \(a = b = 1\), \(c = d = e = 0\). Left side \(X(1, 1, 0) = 1\), right side \(X(1, 0, 0) = 0\). (B) True: if \(a = b\) both sides equal \(a\); if \(a \neq b\) the left side equals its third input \(X(a, b, c)\). (C) False: \(X(a, b, a) = a\) and \(X(c, d, c) = c\), so the right side is \(a\) AND \(c\); with \(a = b = 1\), \(c = d = 0\) the left side is 1 but the right side is 0. (D) True: \(X(a, c, c) = c\), so the right side is \(X(a, m, c)\) with \(m = X(a, b, c)\). If \(a = c\) then \(m = a\) and the result is \(a = m\); if \(a \neq c\) the result is the tie-breaker \(m\).

questions.text: The number \(-6\) can be represented as 1010 in 4-bit 2’s complement representation. Which of the following is/are CORRECT 2’s complement representation(s) of \(-6\)?
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.solution: A 2's complement number is widened by sign extension: copy the sign bit (1) into all new high bits. 1010 becomes 1111 1010 in 8 bits and 1111 1111 1111 1010 in 16 bits. Check: \(-128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 = -6\). Filling with zeros (A, C) gives different values: 1000 1010 is \(-118\).

questions.text: Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE for any binary search tree (BST) having \(n\) distinct integers?

options.label: A
options.text: The maximum length of a path from the root node to any other node is \((n-1)\).

options.label: B
options.text: An inorder traversal will always produce a sorted sequence of elements.

options.label: C
options.text: Finding an element takes \(O(\log_2 n)\) time in the worst case.

options.label: D
options.text: Every BST is also a Min-Heap.

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.chapter: Trees, Binary Search Trees and Heaps
questions.solution: (A) True: a BST with \(n\) nodes has at most \(n - 1\) edges on any root-to-node path, reached by a skewed tree, and no path can be longer. (B) True: inorder visits left subtree, root, right subtree, which is ascending order. (C) False: a skewed BST needs \(O(n)\) comparisons in the worst case. (D) False: in a BST a left child is smaller than its parent, which breaks the min-heap order.

questions.text: A partial data path of a processor is given in the figure, where RA, RB, and RZ are 32-bit registers. Which option(s) is/are CORRECT related to arithmetic operations using the data path as shown?

options.label: A
options.text: The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving two registers.

options.label: B
options.text: The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving one register and one immediate value.

options.label: C
options.text: The data path can implement arithmetic operations involving two immediate values.

options.label: D
options.text: The data path can only implement arithmetic operations involving one register and one immediate value.

questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.chapter: ALU, Data Path and Control Unit
questions.solution: Each ALU input comes from a 2-to-1 multiplexer: Mux_A chooses RA or a 32-bit immediate, Mux_B chooses RB or a 32-bit immediate. Select RA and RB: two registers (A true). Select RA and the immediate on Mux_B (or the immediate on Mux_A and RB): one register and one immediate (B true). Select the immediate on both: two immediate values (C true). Since all three are possible, (D) is false.

questions.text: A regular language \(L\) is accepted by a non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) with \(n\) states. Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE?

options.label: A
options.text: \(L\) may have an accepting NFA with \(< n\) states.

options.label: B
options.text: \(L\) may have an accepting DFA with \(< n\) states.

options.label: C
options.text: There exists a DFA with \(\leq 2^n\) states that accepts \(L\).

options.label: D
options.text: Every DFA that accepts \(L\) has \(> 2^n\) states.

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.solution: (A) True: the given NFA need not be minimal, so a smaller NFA may exist. (B) True: for example, an NFA with redundant states for a simple language can have a DFA with fewer states. (C) True: the subset construction gives a DFA with at most \(2^n\) states. (D) False: it contradicts (C). The only FALSE statement is (D).

questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution: Each I/O operation sends the process to the I/O queue, and when the I/O finishes it returns to the ready queue. The program does 1 scanf and 20 printf calls (the loop runs for i = 0 to 19), so 21 I/O operations. The process enters the ready queue 21 times after its initial entry.

questions.text: Let \(S\) be the set of all ternary strings defined over the alphabet \(\{a, b, c\}\). Consider all strings in \(S\) that contain at least one occurrence of two consecutive symbols, that is, “aa”, “bb” or “cc”. The number of such strings of length 5 that are possible is _______. (Answer in integer)
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution: Total strings of length 5: \(3^5 = 243\). Strings with no two equal adjacent symbols: 3 choices for the first, then 2 for each of the next 4, so \(3 \times 2^4 = 48\). Strings with at least one equal adjacent pair: \(243 - 48 = 195\).

questions.text:
Consider the given function \(f(x)\).

\[f(x) = \begin{cases} ax + b & \text{for } x < 1 \\ x^3 + x^2 + 1 & \text{for } x \geq 1 \end{cases}\]

If the function is differentiable everywhere, the value of \(b\) must be ________. (rounded off to one decimal place)
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution: Differentiable at \(x = 1\) means continuous and with equal one-sided derivatives. Continuity: \(a + b = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3\). Derivatives: left \(a\), right \(3x^2 + 2x = 5\) at \(x = 1\), so \(a = 5\). Then \(b = 3 - 5 = -2.0\).

questions.text: A box contains 5 coins: 4 regular coins and 1 fake coin. When a regular coin is tossed, the probability \(P(head) = 0.5\) and for a fake coin, \(P(head) = 1\). You pick a coin at random and toss it twice, and get two heads. The probability that the coin you have chosen is the fake coin is _______. (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution: \(P(\text{fake}) = 0.2\), \(P(HH \mid \text{fake}) = 1\). \(P(\text{regular}) = 0.8\), \(P(HH \mid \text{regular}) = 0.25\). \(P(HH) = 0.2 + 0.8 \times 0.25 = 0.4\). By Bayes, \(P(\text{fake} \mid HH) = \frac{0.2}{0.4} = 0.50\).

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.solution: fun() is bubble sort, and each swap of adjacent out-of-order elements removes exactly one inversion. An array of 30 distinct values in descending order has every pair inverted: \(\binom{30}{2} = \frac{30 \times 29}{2} = 435\) inversions. So 435 swaps are performed.

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution: z holds the address of a. foo(z, b) receives p = &a and x = 25, and *p = x stores 25 into a. printf prints a, which is 25.

questions.text:
The height of any rooted tree is defined as the maximum number of edges in the path from the root node to any leaf node.

Suppose a Min-Heap \(T\) stores 32 keys. The height of \(T\) is _____________. (Answer in integer)
questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.chapter: Trees, Binary Search Trees and Heaps
questions.solution: A heap is a complete binary tree. Levels 0 to 4 hold \(1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31\) keys, so the 32nd key starts level 5. Height \(= \lfloor \log_2 32 \rfloor = 5\).

questions.text: Consider a memory system with 1M bytes of main memory and 16K bytes of cache memory. Assume that the processor generates 20-bit memory address, and the cache block size is 16 bytes. If the cache uses direct mapping, how many bits will be required to store all the tag values? [Assume memory is byte addressable, \(1K = 2^{10}\), \(1M = 2^{20}\).]
questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.solution: Block offset: 16 bytes \(= 2^4\), so 4 bits. Number of lines \(= \frac{2^{14}}{2^4} = 2^{10}\), so 10 index bits. Tag bits \(= 20 - 10 - 4 = 6\). One tag per line: total \(6 \times 2^{10}\) bits.

questions.text:
A processor has 64 general-purpose registers and 50 distinct instruction types. An instruction is encoded in 32-bits. What is the maximum number of bits that can be used to store the immediate operand for the given instruction?

```text
ADD R1, #25     // R1 = R1 + 25
```
questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.solution: Opcode: 50 instruction types need \(\lceil \log_2 50 \rceil = 6\) bits. Register field: 64 registers need 6 bits. The instruction names one register (R1). Immediate field \(= 32 - 6 - 6 = 20\) bits.

questions.text:
A computer has two processors, \(M_1\) and \(M_2\). Four processes \(P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4\) with CPU bursts of 20, 16, 25, and 10 milliseconds, respectively, arrive at the same time and these are the only processes in the system. The scheduler uses non-preemptive priority scheduling, with priorities decided as follows:

- \(M_1\) uses priority of execution for the processes as, \(P_1 > P_3 > P_2 > P_4\), i.e., \(P_1\) and \(P_4\) have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.
- \(M_2\) uses priority of execution for the processes as, \(P_2 > P_3 > P_4 > P_1\), i.e., \(P_2\) and \(P_1\) have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.

A process \(P_i\) is scheduled to a processor \(M_k\), if the processor is free and no other process \(P_j\) is waiting with higher priority. At any given point of time, a process can be allocated to any one of the free processors without violating the execution priority rules. Ignore the context switch time. What will be the average waiting time of the processes in milliseconds?
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution: At \(t = 0\) both processors are free. \(M_1\) takes its top priority \(P_1\) (0 to 20) and \(M_2\) takes its top priority \(P_2\) (0 to 16). At \(t = 16\), \(M_2\) is free with \(P_3\) and \(P_4\) waiting; by \(M_2\)'s order \(P_3 > P_4\), so \(P_3\) runs 16 to 41. At \(t = 20\), \(M_1\) is free and runs \(P_4\) (20 to 30). Waiting times: \(P_1 = 0\), \(P_2 = 0\), \(P_3 = 16\), \(P_4 = 20\). Average \(= \frac{36}{4} = 9.00\) ms.

questions.text:
Consider two relations describing \(teams\) and \(players\) in a sports league:

- \(teams(tid, tname)\): \(tid\), \(tname\) are team-id and team-name, respectively
- \(players(pid, pname, tid)\): \(pid\), \(pname\), and \(tid\) denote player-id, player-name and the team-id of the player, respectively

Which ONE of the following tuple relational calculus queries returns the name of the players who play for the team having \(tname\) as 'MI'?

options.label: A
options.text: \(\{ p.pname \mid p \in players \land \exists t \, (t \in teams \land p.tid = t.tid \land t.tname = 'MI') \}\)

options.label: B
options.text: \(\{ p.pname \mid p \in teams \land \exists t \, (t \in players \land p.tid = t.tid \land t.tname = 'MI') \}\)

options.label: C
options.text: \(\{ p.pname \mid p \in players \land \exists t \, (t \in teams \land t.tname = 'MI') \}\)

options.label: D
options.text: \(\{ p.pname \mid p \in teams \land \exists t \, (t \in players \land t.tname = 'MI') \}\)

questions.subject: Databases
questions.chapter: Relational Algebra, Tuple Calculus and SQL
questions.solution: p must range over players (it has pname) and t over teams (it has tname). The player must belong to the MI team, so the join condition \(p.tid = t.tid\) is needed along with \(t.tname = 'MI'\). (A) has all of this. (B) and (D) swap the relations, so p.pname and t.tname do not exist. (C) drops the join, so it returns every player whenever a team named MI exists.

questions.text:
A packet with the destination IP address 145.36.109.70 arrives at a router whose routing table is shown. Which interface will the packet be forwarded to?

| Subnet Address | Subnet Mask (in CIDR notation) | Interface |
|---|---|---|
| 145.36.0.0 | /16 | E1 |
| 145.36.128.0 | /17 | E2 |
| 145.36.64.0 | /18 | E3 |
| 145.36.255.0 | /24 | E4 |
| Default | -- | E5 |
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.chapter: IP Addressing, Fragmentation and Support Protocols
questions.solution: Third octet 109 \(= 01101101_2\). /16 with 145.36.0.0: matches. /17: the first bit of 109 is 0, giving 145.36.0.0, not 145.36.128.0, so no match. /18: the first two bits are 01, giving 145.36.64.0, which matches. /24: 145.36.109.0 is not 145.36.255.0. The longest matching prefix is /18, so the packet goes to E3.

questions.text:
Let \(A\) be a \(2 \times 2\) matrix as given.

\[A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\]

What are the eigenvalues of the matrix \(A^{13}\)?
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution: Characteristic equation: \((1 - \lambda)(-1 - \lambda) - 1 = \lambda^2 - 2 = 0\), so \(\lambda = \pm\sqrt{2}\). Eigenvalues of \(A^{13}\) are \((\pm\sqrt{2})^{13} = \pm 2^{6}\sqrt{2} = \pm 64\sqrt{2}\).

questions.text:
Consider the following four variable Boolean function in sum-of-product form

\[F(b_3, b_2, b_1, b_0) = \sum(0, 2, 4, 8, 10, 11, 12).\]

where the value of the function is computed by considering \(b_3 b_2 b_1 b_0\) as a 4-bit binary number, where \(b_3\) denotes the most significant bit and \(b_0\) denotes the least significant bit. Note that there are no don’t care terms. Which ONE of the following options is the CORRECT minimized Boolean expression for \(F\)?
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.solution: Minterms in binary: 0000, 0010, 0100, 1000, 1010, 1011, 1100. \(\bar{b}_1 \bar{b}_0\) covers 0, 4, 8, 12. \(\bar{b}_2 \bar{b}_0\) covers 0, 2, 8, 10. Minterm 11 (1011) is left; pair it with 10 (1010) to get \(b_3 \bar{b}_2 b_1\). All three are essential, so \(F = \bar{b}_1 \bar{b}_0 + \bar{b}_2 \bar{b}_0 + b_1 \bar{b}_2 b_3\). (B) misses 11, (C) misses 4 and 12 and adds 14, 15, (D) adds odd minterms such as 1.

questions.text: Let \(G(V, E)\) be an undirected and unweighted graph with 100 vertices. Let \(d(u, v)\) denote the number of edges in a shortest path between vertices \(u\) and \(v\) in \(V\). Let the maximum value of \(d(u, v)\), \(u, v \in V\) such that \(u \neq v\), be 30. Let \(T\) be any breadth-first-search tree of \(G\). Which ONE of the given options is CORRECT for every such graph \(G\)?

options.label: C
options.text: The height of \(T\) is at least 15.

options.label: D
options.text: The height of \(T\) is at least 30.

questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.chapter: Graph Traversals, Spanning Trees and Shortest Paths
questions.solution: A BFS tree rooted at \(r\) has height equal to the largest \(d(r, x)\). Take \(u, v\) with \(d(u, v) = 30\). By the triangle inequality \(30 \leq d(u, r) + d(r, v)\), so one of them is at least 15, and the height is at least 15. It is at most 30. On a path of 31 vertices (extended to 100 vertices without changing the diameter) the height is 15 from the middle and 30 from an end, so neither 'exactly' option nor 'at least 30' holds for every root.

questions.text:
Consider the following two languages over the alphabet \(\{a, b\}\):

\[L_1 = \{ \alpha\beta\alpha \mid \alpha \in \{a, b\}^+ \text{ AND } \beta \in \{a, b\}^+ \}\]
\[L_2 = \{ \alpha\beta\alpha \mid \alpha \in \{a\}^+ \text{ AND } \beta \in \{a, b\}^+ \}\]

Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT?

options.label: B
options.text: \(L_1\) is a regular language but \(L_2\) is not a regular language.

options.label: C
options.text: \(L_1\) is not a regular language but \(L_2\) is a regular language.

options.label: D
options.text: Neither \(L_1\) nor \(L_2\) is a regular language.

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.solution:
\(L_2\) is regular. A string \(\alpha\beta\alpha\) with \(\alpha = a^k\) starts and ends with \(a\) and has length at least 3. Conversely every such string \(a w a\) with \(w\) non-empty is in \(L_2\) with \(\alpha = a\), \(\beta = w\). So \(L_2 = a(a+b)^+a\), a regular language.

\(L_1\) is not regular. Here \(\alpha\) may be any non-empty string, so a word of \(L_1\) need not start and end with the same letter: \(\alpha = ab\), \(\beta = a\) gives \(abaab\). Intersect \(L_1\) with the regular language \(ab^+aab^+\). A word \(ab^n aab^m\) is in \(L_1\) exactly when some prefix also ends the word, with something in between. The only prefixes that can end in \(b^m\) are \(ab^j\), and \(ab^j\) is also a suffix only for \(j = m\), which needs \(m \leq n\). So the intersection is \(\{ab^n aab^m \mid 1 \leq m \leq n\}\), which is not regular (pumping the \(b^n\) block down breaks \(m \leq n\)). Regular languages are closed under intersection, so \(L_1\) cannot be regular.

So \(L_1\) is not regular and \(L_2\) is regular: option C.

questions.text:
Consider the following two languages over the alphabet \(\{a, b, c\}\), where \(m\) and \(n\) are natural numbers.

\[L_1 = \{a^m b^m c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1\}\]
\[L_2 = \{a^m b^n c^{m+n} \mid m, n \geq 1\}\]

Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT?

options.label: B
options.text: \(L_1\) is a context-free language but \(L_2\) is not a context-free language.

options.label: C
options.text: \(L_1\) is not a context-free language but \(L_2\) is a context-free language.

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.solution: \(L_2\) is context-free: \(S \rightarrow aSc \mid aBc\), \(B \rightarrow bBc \mid bc\); a PDA pushes for each a and b and pops one per c. \(L_1 = \{a^m b^m c^k \mid k > m\}\) needs the number of b's to match a's and the c's to exceed both, two comparisons. Pumping lemma with \(z = a^p b^p c^{p+1}\): the pumped part \(vxy\) has length at most \(p\), so it cannot touch both a's and c's. If it contains a's (and possibly b's), pumping up makes \(m\) grow until the c's are no longer more, or breaks \(\#a = \#b\). If it lies in b's and c's, pumping changes the b count without the a count, or (pumping down c's only) makes \(k \leq m\). So \(L_1\) is not context-free.

questions.text: Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE while computing First and Follow during top down parsing by a compiler?

options.label: A
options.text: For a production \(A \rightarrow \epsilon\), \(\epsilon\) will be added to \(First(A)\).

options.label: B
options.text: If there is any input right end marker, it will be added to \(First(S)\), where \(S\) is the start symbol.

options.label: C
options.text: For a production \(A \rightarrow \epsilon\), \(\epsilon\) will be added to \(Follow(A)\).

options.label: D
options.text: If there is any input right end marker, it will be added to \(Follow(S)\), where \(S\) is the start symbol.

questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.solution: (A) True: if \(A \rightarrow \epsilon\), then \(A\) can derive the empty string, so \(\epsilon \in First(A)\). (B) False: the end marker \(\$\) never belongs to a First set. (C) False: Follow sets contain terminals and \(\$\), never \(\epsilon\). (D) True: the first rule of Follow puts \(\$\) in \(Follow(S)\) for the start symbol.

questions.text:
Consider a relational schema \(team(name, city, owner)\), with functional dependencies \(\{name \rightarrow city, name \rightarrow owner\}\).

The relation \(team\) is decomposed into two relations, \(t1(name, city)\) and \(t2(name, owner)\). Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: The relation \(team\) is NOT in BCNF.

options.label: B
options.text: The relations \(t1\) and \(t2\) are in BCNF.

options.label: C
options.text: The decomposition constitutes a lossless join.

questions.subject: Databases
questions.solution: name determines city and owner, so name is a key of team. Every FD has the key on its left, so team is in BCNF, hence also in 3NF: (A) and (D) are false. In t1 and t2, name is the key and the only FD has it on the left, so both are in BCNF: (B) true. The common attribute name is a key of t1 (and of t2), so the join is lossless: (C) true.

questions.text:
Which of the following predicate logic formulae/formula is/are CORRECT representation(s) of the statement: “Everyone has exactly one mother”?

The meanings of the predicates used are:

- \(mother(y, x)\): \(y\) is the mother of \(x\)
- \(noteq(x, y)\): \(x\) and \(y\) are not equal

options.label: A
options.text: \(\forall x \exists y \exists z (mother(y, x) \land \neg mother(z, x))\)

options.label: B
options.text: \(\forall x \exists y [mother(y, x) \land \forall z (noteq(z, y) \rightarrow \neg mother(z, x))]\)

options.label: C
options.text: \(\forall x \forall y [mother(y, x) \rightarrow \exists z (mother(z, x) \land \neg noteq(z, y))]\)

options.label: D
options.text: \(\forall x \exists y [mother(y, x) \land \neg \exists z (noteq(z, y) \land mother(z, x))]\)

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution:
"Exactly one mother" means: for every \(x\) there is a \(y\) who is the mother of \(x\), and no \(z\) different from \(y\) is a mother of \(x\). (A) False: it only says \(x\) has some mother and someone is not her mother; two mothers are allowed. (B) True: existence plus every \(z 
eq y\) is not a mother. (C) False: it is always true (take \(z = y\)) and asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. (D) True: \(
eg \exists z (z 
eq y \land mother(z, x))\) is equivalent to the uniqueness part of (B).

questions.text:
\(A = \{0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\}\) is the set of non-negative integers. Let \(F\) be the set of functions from \(A\) to itself. For any two functions, \(f_1, f_2 \in F\), we define

\[(f_1 \odot f_2)(n) = f_1(n) + f_2(n)\]

for every number \(n\) in \(A\). Which of the following is/are CORRECT about the mathematical structure \((F, \odot)\)?
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution: Closure: a sum of non-negative integers is non-negative, so \(f_1 \odot f_2 \in F\). Associativity and commutativity follow from those of integer addition. Identity: the zero function \(z(n) = 0\). Inverses: for \(f(n) = 1\) we would need \(g(n) = -1\), not in \(A\), so no inverses in general. Hence it is a commutative (Abelian) monoid but not a group. Only (B) holds.

questions.text: Consider the following deterministic finite automaton (DFA) defined over the alphabet, \(\Sigma = \{a, b\}\). Identify which of the following language(s) is/are accepted by the given DFA.

options.label: A
options.text: The set of all strings containing an even number of \(b\)’s.

options.label: B
options.text: The set of all strings containing the pattern \(bab\).

options.label: C
options.text: The set of all strings ending with the pattern \(bab\).

options.label: D
options.text: The set of all strings not containing the pattern \(aba\).

questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.solution: Name the states \(q_0\) (start), \(q_1\), \(q_2\), \(q_3\) (accepting) from left to right. Transitions: \(q_0\): a to \(q_0\), b to \(q_1\); \(q_1\): b to \(q_1\), a to \(q_2\); \(q_2\): b to \(q_3\), a to \(q_0\); \(q_3\): a to \(q_2\), b to \(q_1\). The states track the longest suffix that is a prefix of bab: \(q_1\) = b, \(q_2\) = ba, \(q_3\) = bab. So exactly the strings ending in bab are accepted: (C) true. (A) False: bbab has three b's and is accepted. (B) False: baba contains bab but ends in \(q_2\), rejected. (D) False: abab contains aba and is accepted.

questions.text: A disk of size 512M bytes is divided into blocks of 64K bytes. A file is stored in the disk using linked allocation. In linked allocation, each data block reserves 4 bytes to store the pointer to the next data block. The link part of the last data block contains a NULL pointer (also of 4 bytes). Suppose a file of 1M bytes needs to be stored in the disk. Assume, \(1K = 2^{10}\) and \(1M = 2^{20}\). The amount of space in bytes that will be wasted due to internal fragmentation is ______. (Answer in integer)
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution: Block size \(= 2^{16} = 65536\) bytes; data per block \(= 65536 - 4 = 65532\) bytes. File size \(= 2^{20} = 1048576\) bytes. 16 blocks hold \(16 \times 65532 = 1048512\) bytes, leaving \(1048576 - 1048512 = 64\) bytes for a 17th block. The last block's data area has \(65532 - 64 = 65468\) unused bytes, which is the internal fragmentation.

questions.text:
Refer to the given 3-address code sequence. This code sequence is split into basic blocks. The number of basic blocks is ________. (Answer in integer)

```text
1001: i = 1
1002: j = 1
1003: t1 = 10*i
1004: t2 = t1+j
1005: t3 = 8*t2
1006: t4 = t3-88
1007: a[t4] = 0.0
1008: j = j+1
1009: if j <= 10 goto 1003
1010: i = i+1
1011: if i <= 10 goto 1002
1012: i = 1
1013: t5 = i-1
1014: t6 = 88*t5
1015: a[t6] = 1.0
1016: i = i+1
1017: if i <= 10 goto 1013
```
questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.chapter: Code Optimisation and Data Flow Analysis
questions.solution: Leaders: the first statement 1001; jump targets 1003, 1002, 1013; statements right after a jump, 1010 (after 1009) and 1012 (after 1011). Leaders in order: 1001, 1002, 1003, 1010, 1012, 1013. Blocks: {1001}, {1002}, {1003 to 1009}, {1010, 1011}, {1012}, {1013 to 1017}. That is 6 basic blocks.

questions.text: A computer has a memory hierarchy consisting of two-level cache (L1 and L2) and a main memory. If the processor needs to access data from memory, it first looks into L1 cache. If the data is not found in L1 cache, it goes to L2 cache. If it fails to get the data from L2 cache, it goes to main memory, where the data is definitely available. Hit rates and access times of various memory units are shown in the figure. The average memory access time in nanoseconds (ns) is ________. (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.subject: Computer Organization and Architecture
questions.solution: From the figure: L1 hit rate 95%, access time 10 ns; L2 hit rate 85%, access time 20 ns including the L1 miss penalty; main memory 200 ns including both miss penalties. Since each time already includes the earlier levels, weight each by the probability the access ends there. \(AMAT = 0.95 \times 10 + 0.05 \times 0.85 \times 20 + 0.05 \times 0.15 \times 200 = 9.5 + 0.85 + 1.5 = 11.85\) ns.

questions.text:
In optimal page replacement algorithm, information about all future page references is available to the operating system (OS). A modification of the optimal page replacement algorithm is as follows:

The OS correctly predicts only up to next 4 page references (including the current page) at the time of allocating a frame to a page.

A process accesses the pages in the following order of page numbers:

1, 3, 2, 4, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3, 1, 4.

If the system has three memory frames that are initially empty, the number of page faults that will occur during execution of the process is ________ . (Answer in integer)
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.solution: 1, 3, 2: three faults filling the frames {1, 3, 2}. The 4th reference, page 4: fault; the window is 4, 2, 3, 1, where 2 is next used first, then 3, then 1, so replace 1: {4, 3, 2}. 2 and 3: hits. Ref 1: fault; window 1, 2, 4, 3: 2 comes first, then 4, then 3, so replace 3: {4, 1, 2}. 2 and 4: hits. Ref 3: fault; window 3, 1, 4: page 2 is not in it, so replace 2: {4, 1, 3}. 1 and 4: hits. Total page faults \(= 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6\).

questions.text:
Consider the following database tables of a sports league.

player(pid,pname,age)
coach(cid,cname)
team(tid,tname,city,cid)
members(pid,tid)

An instance of the table and an SQL query are given.

player

| pid | pname | age |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Jasprit | 31 |
| 2 | Atharva | 24 |
| 3 | Ishan | 26 |
| 4 | Axar | 30 |

coach

| cid | cname |
|---|---|
| 101 | Ricky |
| 102 | Mark |
| 103 | Trevor |

team

| tid | tname | city | cid |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | MI | Mumbai | 102 |
| 20 | DC | Delhi | 101 |
| 30 | PK | Mohali | 103 |

members

| pid | tid |
|---|---|
| 1 | 10 |
| 2 | 30 |
| 3 | 10 |
| 4 | 20 |

```sql
SELECT MIN(P.age)
FROM player P
WHERE P.pid IN (
    SELECT M.pid
    FROM team T, coach C, members M
    WHERE C.cname = 'Mark'
          AND T.cid = C.cid
          AND M.tid = T.tid
    )
```

The value returned by the given SQL query is ______ . (Answer in integer)
questions.subject: Databases
questions.chapter: Relational Algebra, Tuple Calculus and SQL
questions.solution: Mark has cid 102. The team with cid 102 is tid 10 (MI). Members of team 10 are pid 1 and pid 3. Their ages are 31 and 26. MIN(age) \(= 26\).

questions.text: Suppose a 5-bit message is transmitted from a source to a destination through a noisy channel. The probability that a bit of the message gets flipped during transmission is 0.01. Flipping of each bit is independent of one another. The probability that the message is delivered error-free to the destination is ______ . (rounded off to three decimal places)
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution: Each bit arrives correctly with probability 0.99, independently. All 5 correct: \(0.99^5 = 0.95099 \approx 0.951\).

questions.text: Suppose a message of size 15000 bytes is transmitted from a source to a destination using IPv4 protocol via two routers as shown in the figure. Each router has a defined maximum transmission unit (MTU) as shown in the figure, including IP header. The number of fragments that will be delivered to the destination is ________ . (Answer in integer)
questions.subject: Computer Networks
questions.chapter: IP Addressing, Fragmentation and Support Protocols
questions.solution: From the figure: Source to Router-1 (MTU 5000 bytes) to Router-2 (MTU 3000 bytes) to Destination. Take a 20-byte IP header. At MTU 5000 the data per fragment is at most 4980, rounded down to a multiple of 8: 4976. 15000 bytes of data give \(4976 + 4976 + 4976 + 72\), so 4 fragments. At MTU 3000 the data per fragment is at most 2980, a multiple of 8: 2976. Each 4976-byte fragment splits into \(2976 + 2000\), giving 2 fragments; the 72-byte fragment passes as 1. Total \(3 \times 2 + 1 = 7\) fragments reach the destination. Fragments are reassembled only at the destination.

questions.text:
Consider a probability distribution given by the density function \(P(x)\).

\[P(x) = \begin{cases} Cx^2, & \text{for } 1 \leq x \leq 4 \\ 0, & \text{for } x < 1 \text{ or } x > 4 \end{cases}\]

The probability that \(x\) lies between 2 and 3, i.e., \(P(2 \leq x \leq 3)\) is __________. (rounded off to three decimal places)
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.solution: Total probability 1: \(C \int_1^4 x^2 \, dx = C \cdot \frac{64 - 1}{3} = 21C = 1\), so \(C = \frac{1}{21}\). Then \(P(2 \leq x \leq 3) = \frac{1}{21} \cdot \frac{27 - 8}{3} = \frac{19}{63} \approx 0.302\).

questions.text:
Consider a finite state machine (FSM) with one input \(X\) and one output \(f\), represented by the given state transition table. The minimum number of states required to realize this FSM is ________. (Answer in integer)

| Present state | Next state (\(X = 0\)) | Next state (\(X = 1\)) | Output \(f\) (\(X = 0\)) | Output \(f\) (\(X = 1\)) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | F | B | 0 | 0 |
| B | D | C | 0 | 0 |
| C | F | E | 0 | 0 |
| D | G | A | 1 | 0 |
| E | D | C | 0 | 0 |
| F | F | B | 1 | 1 |
| G | G | H | 0 | 1 |
| H | G | A | 1 | 0 |
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.solution: Group by outputs \((f_0, f_1)\): {A, B, C, E} give (0, 0), {D, H} give (1, 0), {F} gives (1, 1), {G} gives (0, 1). Refine {A, B, C, E} by next-state groups: A goes to (F, B) = ({F}, {ABCE}), C to (F, E) = ({F}, {ABCE}), B to (D, C) = ({DH}, {ABCE}), E to (D, C) the same. So split into {A, C} and {B, E}. D and H both go to (G, A), so they stay together. Check again: A and C go to F and to B/E (same group); B and E have identical rows; D and H identical. The partition {A, C}, {B, E}, {D, H}, {F}, {G} is stable: 5 states.

questions.text: Consider the given sequential circuit designed using D-Flip-flops. The circuit is initialized with some value (initial state). The number of distinct states the circuit will go through before returning back to the initial state is _________ . (Answer in integer)
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.solution: The flip-flops form a shift register \(Q_0 \rightarrow Q_1 \rightarrow Q_2 \rightarrow Q_3\) with \(\overline{Q_3}\) fed back to \(D_0\): a 4-bit Johnson (twisted ring) counter. Each clock shifts and complements the bit that wraps round, so after 4 clocks every bit has been complemented once: the state is the complement of the start, never equal to it. After 8 clocks it returns to the start. No shorter cycle is possible (a cycle of length 1, 2 or 4 would make the state after 4 clocks equal the start). So from any initial value the circuit passes through 8 distinct states.

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution: foo adds 1 for every adjacent pair that differs and returns 1 at the last element, so it counts runs of equal values. Array 0, 1, 2, 2, 2, 0, 0, 1, 1: differing pairs are (0,1), (1,2), (2,0), (0,1), which is 4. Result \(= 4 + 1 = 5\) (the runs are 0 | 1 | 2 2 2 | 0 0 | 1 1).

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.chapter: Arrays, Stacks, Queues and Linked Lists
questions.solution: From the figure, L1: 1, 7, 12, 3, 9, 5, 11, 15, 8 and L2: 1, 11, 6, 9, 15, 12, 4. The loop always inspects the node after ptr1, so the head of L1 is never checked. A next node whose value occurs in L2 is unlinked (ptr1 stays put); otherwise ptr1 advances. Values 7, 3, 5, 8 are not in L2 and stay; 12, 9, 11, 15 are in L2 and are removed. The head 1 stays even though 1 is in L2. L1 becomes 1, 7, 3, 5, 8: 5 nodes.

questions.subject: Programming and Data Structures
questions.solution: The first loop stops at t = 100000 (the first power of 10 above 14362), then t = 10000. The second loop takes the digits from the left: 1, 4, 3, 6, 2. turn starts at 0 and alternates, so digits at turn = 1 are kept: the 2nd (4) and 4th (6). newnum = 4, then \(10 \times 4 + 6 = 46\). Output 46.

questions.text: The maximum value of \(x\) such that the edge between the nodes B and C is included in every minimum spanning tree of the given graph is _________ . (answer in integer)
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.chapter: Graph Traversals, Spanning Trees and Shortest Paths
questions.solution: Edges from the figure: AB = 7, AD = 6, DC = 8, BC = \(x\), and the diagonals BD = 1, AC = 3. Edge BC is in every MST exactly when, on every other path from B to C, some edge is strictly heavier than \(x\). Paths: B-D-C has largest edge 8; B-A-C has 7; B-D-A-C has max(1, 6, 3) = 6; B-A-D-C has 8. The smallest of these maxima is 6, so we need \(x < 6\). If \(x = 6\), the MST {BD, AC, AD} of the same weight avoids BC. Largest integer: \(x = 5\).

questions.text:
In a double hashing scheme, \(h_1(k) = k \bmod 11\) and \(h_2(k) = 1 + (k \bmod 7)\) are the auxiliary hash functions. The size \(m\) of the hash table is 11. The hash function for the i-th probe in the open address table is \([h_1(k) + i \, h_2(k)] \bmod m\). The following keys are inserted in the given order: 63, 50, 25, 79, 67, 24.

The slot at which key 24 gets stored is ___________. (Answer in integer)
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.solution: \(h_1\) values: 63 to 8, 50 to 6, 25 to 3, 79 to 2, 67 to 1, all free on the first probe. Key 24: \(h_1 = 24 \bmod 11 = 2\), occupied by 79. \(h_2 = 1 + (24 \bmod 7) = 4\). Probe \(i = 1\): \((2 + 4) \bmod 11 = 6\), occupied by 50. Probe \(i = 2\): \((2 + 8) \bmod 11 = 10\), free. Key 24 goes to slot 10.
